The Quadrilaterals chapter is a high-yield part of the CAT Quantitative Aptitude section, and a favourite in XAT, SNAP, NMAT and CMAT too. This guide explains what CAT Quadrilaterals tests, the formulas and shortcuts worth memorising, the mistakes that cost marks, and a free 10-question online test you can take right now.

Take the quiz below first, read the explanation for anything you miss, then use the chapter e-book at the end for full, exam-level practice.

What CAT asks on Quadrilaterals

Properties and areas of rectangle, square, parallelogram, rhombus and trapezium, and their diagonals.

Key formulas & shortcuts

  • Parallelogram area = base × height; rhombus area = ½·d₁·d₂.
  • Trapezium area = ½(a+b)·h.
  • A square’s diagonals are equal and bisect at 90°.
  • Angle sum of any quadrilateral = 360°.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Using side × side for a rhombus instead of ½·d₁·d₂.
  • Confusing the properties of a rhombus and a rectangle.
  • Forgetting the 360° angle sum.

faq.q: How do you find the area of a rhombus?
faq.a: Half the product of its diagonals: ½·d₁·d₂.

faq.q: How do a rhombus and a rectangle differ?
faq.a: A rhombus has all sides equal and diagonals meeting at 90°; a rectangle has equal diagonals and all right angles.
